Paramour

PAIR-uh-moor · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Paramour is a lover, usually in a secret or improper relationship.

In the novel, the countess risks everything to send one final letter to her paramour before her husband returns from abroad.

Worked Example

In the play, the general secretly visits his paramour every evening after the court has gone to bed, risking his marriage and his title for a few stolen hours.

A paramour is specifically a lover in a relationship that's kept secret or considered improper -- here, one the general is risking everything to keep hidden.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lover: A lover is anyone in a romantic relationship, and the word passes no judgment at all. A paramour is a lover the world is not supposed to know about -- the relationship is secret or considered improper. Every paramour is a lover, but paramour adds the whiff of scandal.

sweetheart: Sweetheart belongs to open, innocent romance -- the word itself sounds wholesome, and no one uses it for an affair that must be hidden. A paramour is the opposite in tone: a lover concealed because the relationship breaks the rules. A high-school sweetheart is public; a paramour never is.

suitor: A suitor courts someone openly and honorably, often with marriage in mind -- introductions to the family, a proposal everyone hopes for. A paramour must stay invisible: the romance is already underway and would cause a scandal if seen. A suitor wants witnesses; a paramour cannot afford any.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

spouse: one's legally married partner

stranger: someone completely unknown or unconnected

Where it sits · how far the romance has gone — admirer → paramour

admirer vs. paramour: An admirer is far earlier on the road than a paramour: an admirer only watches and hopes, perhaps leaving flowers without a name, while a paramour is already deep in a love affair -- one kept secret because it is improper.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — par-

prefix — par-: by, through (Old French)

root — amour

root — amour: love (Old French, from Latin amor)

Put it together

Put it together: Paramour comes from Old French par amour, literally 'by love' or 'for love's sake' -- it originally just meant 'sweetheart,' but narrowed over the centuries to mean a lover in a secret or forbidden relationship.

Use the root in a new word: amorous

Use the root in a new word: amorous: The amorous teenager left a trail of handwritten notes in his crush's locker every day that week.

Word Choice

Paramour carries a slightly old-fashioned, literary flavor and usually implies the relationship is secret or socially disapproved of -- it's rarely used for an openly acknowledged partner.
